utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was not informed of any preliminary matters to be raised. Therefore, we'll wait for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom. Perhaps I could briefly deal with one item which is about Exhibit D1871. On the 30th of May of this year, the Chamber admitted this exhibit into evidence. On 6th of June, the Chamber emailed the parties, noting a discrepancy between the original document and its English translation and requesting that the Defence provide a revised translation. I'll continue with this in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Demurenko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind that you you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Tieger. You'll find Mr. Tieger to your right. Mr. Tieger is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yesterday we had the opportunity to see the video of the press conference you conducted shortly after you completed your investigation and hear your explanation of what had you done. I just want to touch on a few of those specific points that you raised during the conference. First of all, you explained to everyone gathered into the -- to those to whom the film was ultimately disseminated that you used the findings of the investigators who had examined the scene and specifically their findings on the angle of descent and the line of direction to identify the possible locations of the firing point; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the angle of descent that you used was 70 degrees, 7-0; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take into account that I was relying on other people's information, I'm sure, but that doesn't mean that I was able to check those 70 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please answer the question rather than explain matters which are on your mind but apparently not on the mind of the one who examines you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the line of direction that you used was 176 degrees; correct? As you explained during the video.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your leave, I'll just answer briefly using two or three sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to tell Mr. Tieger whether the line of direction that you used was 176 degrees. Did you? Or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you, I used the line on the map that was charted by the previous investigation. I believed what the French and the BH side gave me. The figure didn't matter, 176 or 106. What I used, what mattered, was the line drawn on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just going to ask if you are done with this one, could we please get back to the previous question, to which you had no answer; the 70 degrees question. Once are you done with this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, I'm going suggest to you that the line of direction does matter and I'll be asking you questions about that. But right now, I want to ask you to confirm or deny that almost immediately after you completed your investigation, you told the press conference and, therefore, everybody who was available to listen to it, that you followed a line of direction of 176 degrees. That was your position at the time of the press conference almost immediately after your investigation; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. I stuck to the line, I underline, not degrees, but the line drawn by the previous investigation. It didn't matter to me how many degrees were indicated. You remarked upon it yesterday when I made a mistake and said 106 instead of 176. That doesn't matter. The line on the map matters. Because at the previous session you tried to catch me in a mistake in tables and angles, and different French --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Demurenko, there's no need to start a kind of debate as you just started. Please listen carefully to the questions and answer them. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's assume for the same of this question, and I can tell you that as the parties and the Court is aware, this is reflected in the evidence, that there was more than one line of direction referred to in those reports, so I'm suggesting to that you it's important for purposes of determining what you did to identify which line you followed in your investigation. Do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I followed both lines drawn on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know the -- the -- what those lines represented in terms of degrees? Could you identify them for us in that way? You identified them for everyone who was listening to the press conference, identified as 176 degrees, and then you pointed to another line where you were at a single location, according to the video, that was unspecified. So can you tell what you say those two lines on your video; that is, on the chart you made when you were making the press conference, represented? Did that first line represented 176 as you indicated on the video, as you wrote down on the chart, or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you were able to see in the video, I used only my hand. I didn't use any instrument. My hand cannot draw 170 degrees, and neither can yours. It was just an illustration of what I had done, and it could have been exactly 176 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, tell me if this is a fair characterisation of what I have just heard that you don't know what line you followed, you're just indicating, I followed some line in the course of my investigation and I'm putting down 176 and I'm saying 176 at the time of this press conference as an illustration but it could be anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection. As it mischaracterises the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a question but this is how the answer should be understood. Would you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm answering, no, that's not correct. Because you put it like, do you know which line you followed? I'm answering: I know which line I followed. I know which line I walked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you said earlier it could have been exactly 176 degrees, which I take to mean it could have been something else; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. If you mean to say that I just walked around freely, that's not true. I followed exactly the line drawn on the map given to me by the previous investigators. It was probably exactly 176 degrees as indicated. I didn't check, that was not my purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that you had a question about the angle of descent, the 70 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to insist on getting an answer to your question. Because that question was not answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just going back to the angle of descent of the projectile, is it correct that you relied on an angle of descent of 70 degrees at the time or at least that's what you represented during the press conference?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. I relied - I repeat - on the results of the previous investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then you applied those figures to a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, Mr. Tieger, it's still an ambiguous answer. If you say, I relied on the previous figures, the established figures, was that 70 degree, yes or no; or do you say, I don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I will opt for I don't know because I myself did not measure. I simply believed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you follow a line, even if you have not measured it yourself, then at least you should know, if you say, I relied on the figures established by others, what those figures were. Were those figures 70 degrees, yes or no; or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regardless of the fact that I was repeating those figures, 70 degrees and 176, I still don't know because I didn't take the measurement myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you are now telling us that the figures you followed, as established in the report, were 176 and 70 degrees. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was written, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then you applied those figures to a firing table, the data in a firing table for an M52 120-millimetre mortar; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not correct. I was showing mortar firing tables as a demonstration of the fact that we know that system. I didn't know either the table or the figures. I only needed the line on the map which we physically walked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You didn't use a firing table to make any of the calculations to identify the alleged locations of the firing positions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the assumed firing points, we did use them, but only for them. We just walked the distance. The points themselves didn't matter. It was a demonstration of the fact that we know the weapon. It didn't matter 1200 to 2600, et cetera. We just walked along that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, you said in the video at page 2, paragraph 2 of the transcript of the video, which is D2122, and at approximately 6 minutes and 28 seconds going on into the video itself, you said: "... and in accordance with this angle 70 degrees and this is a direction 176 we can, after comparison with the standard data, see on the following map," and then you went on to identify six and circle -- and write in script the locations of six positions. Now, that appeared to indicate that you used the firing table, that is, the data that you had referred to earlier in the firing table as you held it up on the screen, to identify those six locations. Is that true or not? Or did you come up with those six locations that you circled on the chart in some other way?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, let me repeat, to chart the line of the trajectory, the firing table was not essential and it was not necessary. We used the previous results. To show these six points, the six standard charges that could determine the firing positions emerging from the previous material, yes, we used those tables, but these points did not have any importance for the inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm focussing now on exactly what you said at the time of the video. That is, almost immediately after you completed the investigation. So you have just confirmed that you used a firing table, that's the M52 firing table, correct, that you held up in the video; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I held it up in the video? You mean the table?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You held up the M52 firing table to show what you used when you were conducting your press conference.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I held the firing table.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So I think we've got at least that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have an answer to the question. You -- apart from how you walked, you pointed at certain locations, certain distances from the point of impact. You had that firing table. Did you use that firing table when figuring out where the potential firing positions on that line might have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The table for the 120 millimetre mortar helps determine possible firing positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I really demonstrated them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you use that firing table when even if preliminarily identify possible point of impact points of -- firing points? Did you use that firing table?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to determine the points, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, again, focussing on what your position is, that is what you were asserting almost immediately after your investigation was concluded, you then said you went to the four locations which were on the Bosnian Serb side, those four locations you had drawn on the chart, and you found that each of those spots was "unacceptable or unsuitable for firing position mortar shell." Right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are twisting my words. I said at the press conference that I walked with my own two feet that whole route, including the points that could have been firing positions. I'm talking about my own two feet and the whole route. These words are used in the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you please literally read from the transcript what the witness is recorded as having said. Before you, if you say that Mr. Tieger is twisting your words, then we'll verify what you said as it appears on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So we're now on page 2 of what you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Tieger will now read exactly the words as recorded. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to place it in context --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we are using an exhibit or document, it is customary to have it up on e-court, so the parties know what it is, cite what it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: D2122. That's fair enough. D2122.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a good suggestion to have it in e-court but I think, as a matter of fact, Mr. Tieger referred already to the number of the exhibit. That is the exhibit which was -- it's on the record. But we'll now also see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It has also the transcript attached. Is the English -- there it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we need page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. This is a little harder because this isn't broken down in paragraphs like [indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As we go down the page, toward the middle you see all the numbers and you just explained you used 70 degree, 176 we see them there. Then you identify specific locations, 900 metres, 1400, 2.000, 2700, 3.000 and the last it says church but I think we know that means charge they can use for 3600. Now -- okay. And please move the -- Now, you then said: "Today, personally, with my special, not special, very small investigation group including artillery officers, we was on this place, this place, this, this, and this. Really by my foot. And I can affirm, absolutely without, or beyond any doubts, this is place unacceptable or unsuitable for firing position mortar shell. No perspective stay on this position and shell to this area. And therefore conclusion of material of investigation was wrong." I'm also going to remind you, Colonel, that you circled those specific areas as you were identifying this place, this place, and this. So I put to you again, sir, that what you said at the press conference and what you explained you had done was that you had gone to the specific locations, you had identified on -- already identified on the chart, that ones in the Bosnian Serb area, that is 2000, 2700, 3000 and 3600, this place, this place, this, and this, and asserted that those places were unacceptable or unsuitable for firing a mortar. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that what is written in the text corresponds to what I said. Maybe the problem is in the translation. Twice it was said, you went.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's remark: The Russian verb "to go" differs depending whether you use a vehicle or your own two feet. And the colonel is now saying that "went" in English was translated as if he had been using a vehicle, where he actually walked all the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We got information from the interpreters about the use of certain Russian words. Now, whether that explains everything is still to be verified. We do understand that you confirm -- by the way, it's not a matter of translation because you confirmed what you said at the press conference but you've added today several times, although you didn't say it at the time, that you went on foot along the whole of the trajectory as defined by that line. That's how --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On my own two feet and that's written in the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and that's on foot. I understand that you do that with two feet, not with one. But that's, you say you did at the time, and Mr. Tieger was asking you questions about what you said during the press conference. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's look now at what you next explained about this at least next in the -- as far as we have access -- I won't say next, but let's just look at what you said in 2007 to the Dragomir Milosevic Trial Chamber about your investigation. First of all, you explained to the Milosevic Trial Chamber, as you had in the -- in the press conference, that you used the data of experts which allowed you to chart the line that allows -- that -- that provides possible firing points; right? You used the expert data?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object. Again, this is day one in this trial when we cite to other cases, we get a transcript reference so it can be checked by the parties so we can see if the wording is accurate. I don't why we're departing from that tradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not making a specific -- I'm not quoting the witness, I'm not showing him what he said, I'm asking him if he doesn't know, then I'll go to something specific and I'll ask him whether or not that's true. But I think I'm entitled to ask the witness if he recalls what he said, especially because he signed the amalgamated statement -- attested to an amalgamated statement that contains large portions of that testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, then we can go to the statement but to give a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's fair to start asking the witness the gist of what he testified before and then later, perhaps with technical means, that is, transcripts, to verify the answer and to further test the reliability and the credibility of what the witness now testifies about in court. Certainly, Mr. Ivetic, at some point in time, if it becomes an issue, then certainly we'll carefully and closely look, and if Mr. Tieger doesn't spontaneously do it, we'll invite him to look at that transcript. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So that's my question, Colonel. Did you explain to the Dragomir Milosevic Trial Chamber that you relied on the data of experts, specifically the angle of descent and the line of direction, to chart a line on which you could identify possible firing points?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I supposed to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally I cannot remember verbatim what was said nine years ago, but I take your word for it that I had said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Well, since this question has arisen, let's turn to 65 ter 33683, e-court page 10. This is you answering, sir. Your answer is: "A. Yes, but it's only when you have in front of you reports from specialists who used specialised tools in their work who calculated possible angles of descent. Only with that using firing tables, takes into account that angle and the bearings can you chart the line which allows to check possible firing points." So, as you had explained in the press conference, you told the Dragomir Milosevic Trial Chamber that you used the angle of descent and the line of direction from the investigators and the firing table to chart -- to follow a line on which you considered you could find possible firing points; right.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. Speaking about the angle of descent and the direction of the possible trajectory of the shell and repeating those figures, I meant that they were taken from the previous investigation, but I never said anywhere that only these figures led me to investigate what I did on site. It was just an argument to show that I didn't just take these figures out of nowhere. I used previous investigators' documents, but it doesn't mean that I relied only on them for my own investigation. Those were just lines that I had to investigate, among others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you a perhaps relatively simple question. If all these locations are not of that importance, why didn't you say, I checked the whole of the trajectory line where distances are totally irrelevant apart than it could not be closer than a minimum, and could not be further than a maximum. You, both in the Dragomir Milosevic quote, and in the press conference, you were not focussing on the whole of the line, but you explained that there were, on the basis of the tables, certain points that you inspected. Why did you refer to those points rather than said, I went through the whole of the line, which may be 2 kilometres, 3 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's understandable why. For military professionals, not amateurs, it's quite clear that firing positions could not just be anywhere. They had to be consistent with the technical features of that particular mortar. That's why I spoke about these particular points. But my words to the effect that I went on my feet the whole distance was to say that my task was to walk the whole route to establish there had been no mortars anywhere there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Couldn't firing positions be anywhere on that line, if not below the closest distance and not further away than the maximum reach of the weapon system? They could be anywhere or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Absolutely. They could have been at any point along that line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now you're telling us, at least if I understood you well, that in order for the public to fully understand, you pointed at specific locations, whereas, if I understand you well, you say, That's not what it is. It's the whole of the line. So why draw the attention of the public to four specific spots where you, as a professional, understand that it's not about these specific spots but it's just the whole of the line? I still do not understand what you wanted to explain to the public to better understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, it's all very simple. I had only a few minutes for that interview. If you had had an hour or two, I would have in great detail described that whole weapon, how it fires, what positions are possible, and everything. I had to put a maximum of information into two, three minutes, including the view of the city to make it more plain, more demonstrative. And, indeed, only the specialists were involved in this work, whereas, that programme was meant for laypeople.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would then not it have been the simplest way to explain by saying, This is the direction where it came from. I inspected the whole of that line, and there was no spot which was suitable for firing. Which would saved you a lot of time for this long interview -- this short interview because you didn't have to calculate and show the tables, et cetera. It would have saved a lot of time. So I'm still puzzled by your explanation that this was the way to save time and to better explain what you say is not exactly what professionals would think. If you want to add something fine; if not, then I'll ask Mr. Tieger to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please one minute, one comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I gave you an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely agree with you, but at that time, I was just a field commander, a regular field commander. I was not a PR specialist. If I had that opportunity all over again, I would have done much better in keeping with your advice and my experience since then. I had no experience then with talking to the media, and I had not been prepared as I am for -- for this session or my appearance at a previous trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, you seem to have focussed on the relatively short time you claim you had during the press conference, but I'm suggesting to that you when you came to testify in the Dragomir Milosevic, which encompassed several days, you emphasised, among other things, two things: Number one, that you followed a specific line of direction; and, number two -- specific line of direction rather than canvassing the entire slope. And, number two, that you focussed on specific locations. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's what I said. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I may return to that -- well, we'll see in a moment. Let me -- Now, at paragraph 121 through 123 of your amalgamated statement, you address the Dragomir Milosevic Trial Chamber's rejection of your conclusions about the -- about following your investigation, rather. And you say they got confused. Do you recall that portion of your amalgamated statement or do you need to see that again?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I answer now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I not simply agree with that. I was emphasizing to myself even that the expertise of the people at this Tribunal, specifically the Office of the Prosecutor, and, of course, I got confused because I was getting such masterful questions, so sophisticated questions, that I was not always able to follow the logic of these questions as a military man, and I am specialised only in military matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Tieger, you said: "I was explained the finding of the Dragomir Milosevic Trial Chamber in relation to my evidence in that case." Did you read the judgement or was it just conveyed to you, or did you receive a translation? Could you tell us exactly what you were -- knew about that judgement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just trusted what I was told. I didn't check anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Told by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe they told me, but I just don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know who explained to you what was found -- to be found in the Dragomir Milosevic Trial Chamber's judgement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After my appearance at that trial, I never saw any materials about it. I never read anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you felt free to tell that the Trial Chamber was wrong in its understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you are now, again, quoting back my comments, it's obvious that I had not been able to argue my points and show that I was right. It just shows the artfulness of the other party when they are catching me out, using tables, using different materials. You can see the -- the art they are using in their work. I am not artful in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not exactly an answer to my question, but, Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, you stated and have affirmed to this Court in paragraph 121 of your amalgamated statement, D2120, that it is not -- that your evidence in the Dragomir Milosevic case "was not accepted because I allegedly did not investigate the entire possible area where Serb mortars could have been located and fired from at Markale II." And then you go ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the part that has been read by counsel is not a quotation in verbatim format of what the witness actually said. Which begins with: "Also I was told that this determination was consistent with the Prosecution's line of my cross-examination that Colonel Demurenko confined himself to too narrow an area in seeking to identify the possible launching positions. In other words ..." and then what Mr. Tieger said. If we present what the witness said, we should present what the witness actually said and not what Mr. Tieger wishes he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the witness paraphrased by saying in other words and that Mr. Tieger is perfectly allowed to rely on the way in which the witness himself rephrased his previous testimony? "In other words," that is what the witness says in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. But Mr. Tieger is not saying "in other words." He is saying this is what's written in the statement and it's not. It is only half of what is in the statement in relation to what the witness said in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You never read the whole of the statement if you say this is what is stated here. You choose your portion and then in re-examination, you can put the other part to the witness apart from -- I think the appropriate way of trying to get the whole of it in is to invite Mr. Tieger, say, Mr. Tieger, could you please also read the previous four lines to the witness and that takes less time than the way in which it is done now. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The fact is, Colonel, as you just acknowledged a few moments ago, that it was you, during your Dragomir Milosevic Chamber [sic] who focussed on the precision or specificity of locations you examined.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And where is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you, sir, that the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber was not confused as say in paragraph 122 about whether you claim to have scoured the entire slope of the mountain for possible firing points rather than focussing on specific locations but that you yourself emphasised during your Dragomir Milosevic Chamber that your investigation was predicated upon the fact that you had identified and examined specific locations.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I walked the whole line, focussing on certain points. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 33683, page 41, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. You can see here you're asked a question about what you talked about in your TV appearance. Went through these rocky areas, determined it was impossible to fire. When did you go. You say: "I understand now." Explained there was several of you, perhaps somebody else joined you. Then you go on to say: "The principle was quite simple. We were to look at the fire tables and co-ordinate in order to establish with a margin of error of 1 to 2 metres the exact location." If we turn four pages from there to page 7781 of the transcript, page 45 in e-court. "Q. Very well. And what you did, and you explained it nicely on the chart behind you, is you followed this or looked at these four possible locations which were on the Bosnian Serb side which correspond to the possible charges used to fire that shell, namely charge three, four, five, and six. "A. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move down. One second. Mr. Tieger is still reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And so -- and the question, the next question is: "Q. So the guiding principle for you to look at these locations was this line of 176 degrees. "A. Both the line and the angle. The angle indicated the exact locations of fire points." And perhaps one more example, at ... 3368 -- 65 ter 33684, e-court page 51. And this is questioning by Defence counsel, Mr. Tapuskovic. He asks you about photographs: "...and I'll show you just a couple of more. Each of those photographs depicts one such possible firing position. "A. That's precisely how it was. Each photograph was made in one particular occasion which had been identified in advance with a margin of error of 5 metres. My team and I travelled to these locations and took these photographs precisely in order to show that it was impossible to fire from there." And then I'll just continue. "You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "You mentioned that explicitly earlier. In the vicinity of this location where you took this photograph, were you able to observe the entire area? Were you able to see whether there were any traces showing that a 120-millimetre mortar was placed in that area? "A. Certainly, as we were approaching this spot, we observed the entire area around it, and had I seen 10 to 20 metres away from this spot a possible firing position, then, yes, this could have been something that could have prompted me to draw some other conclusions in my investigation. However --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "However, there were no such traces anywhere." Those portions of your testimony reflect, do they not, Colonel, your emphasis on the precision of your identification of the alleged potential or possible points of firing; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not denying anything that's shown in the transcript. More attention was paid to these points simply because questions were asked constantly about these points, but that doesn't mean that the rest of the route had not been inspected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demurenko, could I ask you the following. One of the portions that was read to you was whether you were guided by the line of the direction, and then, without any further question, you said, Not only the line but also the angle so as to be better able to find the locations. So where you now say that in the questioning the focus was on the spots but that you inspected the whole of the line, you yourself corrected one question which was focussing on the whole of the line by saying, Well, not only the whole of the line but the specific positions. So to say, I was led to do this by the questions, that seems to be an example, but if I understand it wrongly, please explain it to me, that it was you yourself who moved away from the whole of the line to a specific position. Do you have any comment on what I think I read in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now and then I'm saying the same thing. I walked that line. Attention was paid on certainly points, but, still, it was the whole line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Given the time, Mr. President, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll move on after the break. Mr. Demurenko, you may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll just continue where I stopped at the beginning of this session when I was dealing with Exhibit D1871. I told you that we informed the parties about the discrepancy between the original of the English translation. Now, on 13th of June, the Defence informed the Chamber and the Prosecution by e-mail that it had uploaded a revised translation into e-court. The Prosecution responded that same day, noting that it had no objections to the revised translation, and the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the existing translation of Exhibit D1871 with the document up loaded under doc ID 1D31-0739.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if you are ready, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, before we broke, we were discussing your testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case and looking at some of your comments there, as well as paragraphs 121 through 123 of your amalgamated statement. During the course of the testimony in the Karadzic case, you were asked, after you had explained as you did here this morning, that you searched the whole area, why you didn't say to the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber that you covered the entire area, and you explained in response that, It was because they probably didn't ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that connection, if we could turn to 65 ter 33680, e-court page 49. Two pages past, please. It's transcript page 28931.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, and this is the backdrop to your comment as we see here, so with the opportunity to tell the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber , indeed not just an opportunity but an obligation because the Judge was asking you that very question, you didn't say that you went -- you covered the entire area for thousands and thousands of metres around. You said: Look, we looked at the precise spot and the 20 to 30 metres around it in order to determine that the mortar couldn't have been fired from there, and that's why the Milosevic chamber" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "And that's why the Milosevic chamber reached the conclusion it did. Isn't that right?" Your answer is: "I'll answer that. Concerning the first part," now, that's about an issue related to a [indiscernible] which is not in response to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Could we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And there we see at the second paragraph: "The second thing: Why I didn't talk more about the area we covered. As a professional - not in geology but in another area of expertise - it's difficult for me to explain why I didn't speak about it. Perhaps they didn't ask me. They probably didn't ask me." And then you go on to say: "But I have to say that in the interview on the video I said that we explored the locality. I didn't say a particular location or point. We explored the locality, and that means that we explored a large area lest we later be accused of a biased conclusion. And that's all I have to say." Now -- okay. And I take it you stand by the accuracy of that transcript, that is, that reflects what you said to the Karadzic Chamber; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubt about this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So with respect to your explanation that you didn't talk about the vast area you had allegedly covered but instead focussed on specific areas because they "didn't ask me, they probably didn't ask me," I'd like to look at an exchange in the Dragomir Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to 65 ter 33682, e-court page 48, please. Can you scroll up, please, so I can see that page number. If we can turn back one page, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, this is immediately after the playing of the press conference video that we saw here in court and its admission, and then one of the Judges at the bottom of the page asked -- asks for some clarification. And if we continue to the next page, please. And he says: "You said, I think, several times during your interview in the footage that it would have been impossible for anyone to fire a mortar grenade from those areas depicted on or indicated on your line going down 176 degrees. Because you said that there were hills and forests, I believe, and it would be impossible to fire a mortar grenade from anywhere in that area. That's how I understood it. But I'm not sure I understand why would it be impossible. A mortar grenade, I suppose, can be fired from many places and -- and if there's a clearance in the woods or if there's a road, then you can probably fire it from there. "So what supported your conclusion that it would have been impossible to fire a mortar from anywhere in that area? Just explain to us very briefly. Thanks." You make apologies for your poor English and you say you will try to do it shortly. And then you say in response: "120-millimetre mortar is very specific, very old type of weapon. Really this is tape and tube. No special equipment for very, very specific point of firing. And as you know maybe, we have this type of weapon, only six charges. It's a specific small back with explosion. The principle of the firing for a mortar, this is a tape, this is a tube and we can to change this angle only on the vertical, not on horizontal and six charges. And therefore during the maximum multiple horizontal, for example, 89 degrees and like this, and one charges, the maximum parabola" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "... if we will have this angle as a minimum, for example, 30 -- 30 degrees and the six charges of this. If this is a parabola, but a little bit other like this. And in Sarajevo, in this incident, it was absolutely clear that this is the -- two building, this is the crater, this is the terrain, this is boundary, confrontation line, this is BiH, this is the Serbian. Both sides. "And we know exactly in accordance with data of expert, I don't know -- approximately 60, 70 he degree, maybe 70, I forget it, but all the same now. And in this case, I mean this angle, this angle has therefore only one, two, three, four, five, six point for firing position, and we inspected each -- I mean on Serbian side, even on confrontation line each position with photoparat in each of these firing positions, it was stones. It's not road. It's stones. Absolutely impossible to stay plate on the stones. In accordance with military point of view, absolutely impossible. And one position is the forest, the mine can't move through there, the part of the trees, because blast immediately. "Therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Therefore, we check it on the photoparat photo, each four positions and five position with other angle. Do you remember from this point? No inspection of the BiH." And then you said: "We said, okay, maybe could be next step for us, but absolutely clear 100 per cent that Serbs can't organise the provided shelling from this position according with this angle. Angle is no without doubt, because expert, ballistic expert. "That's all. It is it clear, more or less." Now, the Judge continued to press for an answer and said: "But Colonel would there not be quite a large margin around each of these six firing points and even so, the further out you get, the larger the margin within which the fire could have been shot is increased? So if you take the example with the six charges" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "That -- I mean, if it was fired from there, it could have been fired, I suppose, quite a large area. It did not necessarily have to be fired from the position where you were and you took the photograph. If, for instance, a couple of hundred metres away there would have been a road or something else, the shot could have come from there. So are you able really to exclude that the mortar could not have been fired each from an area adjacent to the place where you were?" And this is what you said to the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber : "I want [sic] to emphasise one thing once again. I know this weapon very, very well. Maybe my -- maybe the interpretation of the word charge was misleading. There are no different shell, six shells there. There are six charges. And it's charged manually. You put the shell inside the tube and it flies up. "So the firing tables for the mortars that you saw in that video footage show that in that direction only six charges are possible, either one, two, three, all the six were taken into account. Margins of deviation are measured in metres, like 10 to 15 metres, the size of this room, but the margin of deviation cannot be 100 metres. We took into account ballistic trajectories. It's the science of physics. We cannot go beyond that. "If you take a certain line of fire, only six possible firing points exist, depending on the charges used. We photographed an area of 20 to [sic] 30 square metres. We always proceeded from a certain surface on which the mortar had to rely. It cannot hang in the air. It cannot be suspended on a tree. We showed the photographs and we saw the ground was pure, clear. No mortar had stood there." Now, first of all, Colonel, I take it that you do not dispute the accuracy of what was recorded of your words in that transcript. That's an accurate reflection of what you said. Correct.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not doubting the materials before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, therefore, Colonel, contrary to your suggestion that you had failed to explain the wide area you covered in your investigation because the Dragomir Milosevic Trial Chamber probably didn't ask you about that, in fact, the Trial Chamber focussed you directly and repeatedly on precisely that issue, and you continued to emphasise that you went, you were -- you had calculated with precision the possible areas of fire and went to those locations where you determined, according to you, it was impossible to fire. That's the truth about your testimony in the Milosevic case; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can put different interpretations on my testimony as you wish. I said then and I'm saying now that our objective was not to find firing positions. Our task was to refute the lie that had been presented as the truth previously. We did not find the firing positions, so it was a lie about Serbian aggression. All the rest was a repetition of the previous lie about the Serbian aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, during the course of the Karadzic case, you conceded that the Dragomir Milosevic Trial Chamber was not confused by margins of error but understood you to be saying exactly what you were saying that you focussed on very precise locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that connection, let me turn to 65 ter 33680, e-court page 48.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Tieger, I have a question for the witness. You just said, and I quote: "Our task was to refute the lie that had been presented as the truth previously ..." Who gave you this task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To unmask the lie, nobody gave me that task. I put it to myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But would that mean, on from the beginning you knew it was a lie and you only had to establish that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course not. My position was one of impartiality, and it was true then it remained. If we had found the firing positions along that line, I would have certainly confirmed it, recognised it, and I would have said so plainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have another question. Let me see, I need to find it. Let me ... I'll find it in a second. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we scroll up, please. Yeah, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, this is your testimony in the Karadzic case. You can see at the top I'm asking you about what you said previously about precise locations, exact locations, et cetera. And then, about midway through the page at line 17, I -- you were asked: "So Colonel, I put it to you that the Dragomir Milosevic Trial Chamber was not confused about the two different kinds of margins of error reflected in the tables you put into your amalgamated witness statement, but they understood you to be saying exactly what you were saying, that you were focussed on very precise locations. That is the testimony you gave to the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber , isn't it? " And you said: "Let me respond. That's right, because otherwise had I covered the map with my hand and said I investigated this entire area, it would not have sound convincing." And then you go on to say: "One needs to be precise in military [sic] sense, et cetera" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "In the artillery sense, precise and show everything that is open for calculation, that is, that can be calculated. So what we investigated were specific locations and I covered -- I spoke about all of them in quite precise terms because we had to show that we knew how to make calculations using the known angles in order to define the possible firing points. However, let me draw your attention to the fact that that doesn't exclude the possibility that not only 10 to 15 metres further, but 150 metres further and 200 metres further, everything was thoroughly investigated and photographed. And one doesn't contradict the other. Have I answered your question?" So, again, Colonel, this accurately reflects what you said in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that I have no doubts about the records from the previous trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And in that case, you confirmed that rather than explaining to the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber that you covered vast amounts of area, that you were focussed on very precise locations and you explained that that was correct because otherwise had you covered the map with your hand and said you investigated the entire area, that wouldn't have sounded convincing. That was your position in the Karadzic case; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm now having difficulty, all day today. The difficulty is this: From the very beginning, I've said that I, indeed, stand by all that I said before. However, interpretations of my words are completely different between Mr. Tieger and I. I was saying one thing, and he keeps highlighting something entirely different. And that's where the trouble starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you have explained where the trouble starts. But could you perhaps also answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm ready. Please give me the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether what Mr. Tieger put to you as your position in the Karadzic case, whether that was right or not. And I'll read it again to you. Mr. Tieger put to you in the Karadzic case you confirmed that rather than explaining to the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber that you covered vast amounts of area that you were focussed on very precise locations and that you explained that that was correct because otherwise had you covered the map with your hand and said you investigated the entire area, that wouldn't have sounded convincing. Whether that was your position in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. We focussed on a particular line and certain points on that line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it's a precise answer to the question, but I -- I have the following question for you. You talked about the calculations. What calculations were made in your team? I mean, you had the angle of descent. You had the direction of the origin of fire. What else did you calculate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, we had a map with the line of possible firing already drawn. We didn't draw it. Then we took one line, that line, and the additional line, the possible line of descent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The angle of direction. And after that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Possible line of descent." Could you explain to me what you mean with "possible line of descent"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant angle of descent that was written by the BH experts on the map. And the direction that we were given. Why am I saying possible? Because nobody before investigating could either confirm or refute. They just drew a line and said it was the Serbs. And I put a task to myself. Let's see if it was indeed the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was what exactly you calculated. I do understand that you took into account the angle of descent, that you took into account the line of the origin of fire as plotted on a map. I did understand that you also consulted the tables for this mortar. Did you consider anything else when calculating what may have been the origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If you mean documents, we used the table; and if you mean instruments, we used the artillery compass with which we used to -- with which we -- we tried to get the same line we saw on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I didn't mean that, as a matter of fact. Because you're now talking about the instruments or the -- but what I'm talking about is: Did you take into account in your calculations anything else than angle of descent, direction of the origin of fire, and the data as contained in the tables? Did you consider anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not that I remember. There was no need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the possible locations, the distances from the point of impact, was that established on the basis of these tables, taking into account the line of the origin of fire and the -- and the angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The line of fire and the angle of descent were given to us. We didn't calculate that ourselves. And the possible firing points, yes, we calculated them, according to the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not a real calculation. That's just looking up this angle of descent, so many charges, would result in this and this and this. It's, rather, consulting the tables than making any calculations, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, consulting the table is the preparation for artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mortar is the most basic primitive weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see your point. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, as long as we're focussed at the moment on consulting the firing table, let's take a look at that, Colonel. Now, just a few moments ago at page 30 and yesterday in the video of the press conference, you emphasised your knowledge of the weapons system. And I believe that yesterday, at about transcript page 4489 [sic] or so, you referred to your -- 44088, you referred to your mastery of the weapon, so I want to ask you some questions about the firing tables that you used or didn't use. First of all, you assumed in the course of the exercise you conducted that the calculations that you obtained from the M52 firing table could be used to identify the precise locations from which the mortar was potentially fired; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The key word you are using is "could be"; right? Or potentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you used -- it was the M52 firing table that you relied on to identify what you described to the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber as the precise locations from which a mortar which landed at that angle might have been fired from on that particular line of direction; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The key word is "particular line," points are of secondary importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you were shown in the Karadzic case a document reflecting that the inventory of the VRS included not only M52 120-millimetre mortars but M74 and M75 millimetre mortars. And you affirmed that was consistent -- you didn't dispute that, right, you agreed that that was accurate for purposes of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this -- I didn't get an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: 120 millimetres. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, just trying to shortcut this because I showed you this document in the Karadzic case and you didn't dispute it. But if you have a problem with that I'll show you the document. That's a document reflecting that the inventory of the VRS included not just M52 120-millimetre but also M74 120-millimetres and M75s; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not denying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then when you were asked in the Dragomir Milosevic case, whether you were aware of evidence about an M74 mortar system along with an M52, you said: It's one and the same system, regardless of whether it's an M52 or an M74, it's one and the same gun with the same firing tables. First of all, do you remember that testimony or do you want me to show you the portion of the transcript where you said that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And that's similar to what you told the Trial Chamber yesterday, that all these systems are essentially the same and there's -- you can use -- you can rely on one firing table interchangeably with the others because the data in those firing tables is going be to -- essentially the same; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not denying my own words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And for that reason, you didn't check a firing table for an M74, and you didn't check a firing table for an M75; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for that. Those were secondary firing points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, Witness, whether there was any need to do that is not the question. The question is whether you did compare them. Did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me answer. In that case, you need to invite my whole investigating group and examine my artillery officers, how in depth they actually calculated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. It's not for you to tell us whom to address with our questions. I did put this question to you and I asked you whether you compared the two tables, the one table you had in your hands when you gave the interview and a table for an M74 or an M75. My question is: Did you compare them? So did you; did you not; or don't you know; on don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 289 -- sorry. 65 ter 33681, e-court page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, there, you were asked the following question: "In any event, based on your responses, it appears that you did not check any firing tables [sic] for mortars in making your calculations other than the M52 firing table. You didn't check a firing table for an M74, you didn't check a firing table for an M75; is that right?" --

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm reading -- oh, it's not right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said a moment ago that I don't know whether my artillery officers checked other tables or not. I just said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I remind you that I asked you whether you did it. Whether you did it, whether you didn't do it or whether you didn't remember. And then you said: I don't remember. I didn't ask you about that team. You introduced that. Would you please focus on the question asked and not on the question which you may have on your mind. And you interrupted Mr. Tieger when he was reading a portion of the transcript. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm told there might be an issue with translation in the Russian language, "you" can be translated in the plural as well. So, by you saying "you," it's not the same meaning as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at what exactly the transcript tells us. One second, please. The witness moved away from the question when he talked about inviting his whole team to give an answer to that question. I then interrupted him and I said, Well, don't tell us whom we should ask the questions. I asked you whether you compared the two tables, the one table you had in your hand or not. And it's theoretically possibly that after -- in this course of events, the witness still thinks on the basis of language that I could have referred to the plural although by stopping him it was, I think, perfectly clear to the witness that I was not interested in what others may have done but in what he did. I leave it to that at this moment. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just completed repeating -- witness, you have your hand up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Demurenko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until this moment, I thought that when you are saying "you," what is meant is me and my group. If that is not so, then you should say "you personally." I personally didn't make photos. I personally did not make calculations. My group did everything. In that case, you should always formulate things as you personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will try to formulate our questions as precisely as possible, but I'll check with my colleagues whether it would have been -- should have been clear to you that when I interrupted you when you referred me to members of your team, whether, in the follow-up question, it was clear enough that I meant you, but we'll use you personally in the near future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You could also understand that when you're asked if you did something that it means you and if the intention is to include your group we would say did you and your group do the following. So you can understand "you" to mean you. We were talking to you. We were not talking to your group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we'll try to avoid whatever confusion there may be, and it's good that you have expressed -- and that we are now aware that "you" can be used both, as in English, in the singular and the plural. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I had just finished repeating to you what had been asked you in the Karadzic case. "You didn't check a firing table for an M74. You didn't check a firing table for an M75; is that right?" And on 17th of October, 2012, you said: "Yes, that's correct." You continue: "The principle that I followed was quite simple, to unmask the initially wrongly made conclusions. I started from what you say in my sketch, a shell and then the mortar, et cetera. My task was to show that that was a lie. I had no other goal. It wasn't my objective to establish what actual weapon was used to fire the shell, et cetera, et cetera. That's the task for police, for ballistics expert, and so on." So the fact is, that you testified in 2012 that the M74 and the M75 firing tables had not been consulted in the course of this exercise; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you had no idea whether or not your team did -- you're smirking, Colonel. Why is this so funny?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it was a question. If you want to answer, you can. If you don't, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just smiling ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there is a problem with the channels at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, it changes the logic of the first two trials and our trial. The majority of the questions was formulated as "you." I didn't take it always that I personally am meant. A Colonel doesn't write all the instructions out. His team does that. So in future, it would be simpler to specify "you personally."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have repeated that now. But could I ask you now the following. Did your team consult the other tables?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Quite possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if the question was put to you, you didn't check a firing table for an M74. You didn't check a firing table for an M75; is that right? And you answered in the affirmative, yes, that's correct, now, if you understood "you" as being you personally, which, apparently, you didn't do, then it means that you have not consulted the firing tables yourself. If you understood you didn't check a firing table to be you, the team, then you apparently also confirmed that that's correct, meaning that the team did not consult the firing table. So, therefore, in both cases, when you confirmed, you included your team, whereas, now you say I don't know. I just did put this to you. Mr. Tieger, any further questions now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, if anyone had consulted the M74 and M75 firing tables and if those firing tables were not exactly the same in terms of the data contained as the M52, then that would have resulted in more than six possible positions based on six possible charges; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But your position is they're exactly the same and so it didn't matter anyway; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it doesn't matter because the line is the same. It's 50 metres to one side or to the other, but the line is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I wondered about the 50 metres but perhaps you can explore that on the basis of the tables given by the witness in his statement. And I'm specifically referring to - let me see - to Table 1 in paragraph 122. You may address that. I will wait. Where the witness said 50 metres to the left or to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to follow up on this in the questions I have been focussing on now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, you were the person who said --

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't say to the left or to the right. I said closer or further on the line. Only the line matters. I didn't mean to the left or to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I, indeed, used words you didn't use because as it was translated to us, you said - let me see - You said 50 metres to one side or the other which is commonly understood as left and right. But if you intended to say closer or further, that's fine, then we know what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, irrespective - and we'll talk about that - of anything else following from what the firing tables may or may not show, you're the person who told this Chamber and the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber that you knew this system very, very well, that you had mastery of the system and assured everyone that there was no difference in the firing tables for these three types of weapons. So why don't we look at what the firing tables actually show. And in that respect, if I could call up 65 ter 33827, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, are we having a question or are we having commentary by Mr. Tieger. If it is commentary, I object and ask for it to be stricken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's an introduction to the question, I think. He reminded the witness of part of his testimony as an introduction to his next question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, what we see on the screen, Colonel, is an excerpt from P7539 which is a firing table, I believe, for an M74, but the reason I'm showing you this is that this portion of the firing table contains a chart showing the correspondence of degrees in mils. And the reason I'm showing that is because we'll see the reference to distances reflected in the other portions of the table in mils. So if we look down the degrees until we get to the last item in the fifth row down, we see 70 degrees. And if we look to the right, we see that in the system used by the JNA, which corresponds to this table we have 1166 mils. 1166.67 to be exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm sorry that is not highlighted, other portions will be. But if you look at the various aggregations of degrees, beginning with 46 through 50 on top, and then you go down the little combinations from 46 then to 51 then to 56 then to 61, until you get down to 70, and then you scroll right across you see 1166 mils.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw that you used the word row which in tables is used in a different way. You were talking about the fifth group under the heading "degrees," and then the last item which says 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you see that, Colonel? And that's the way to look at the firing tables and if you see mils, you know what -- what -- if you know the degree, then it's translated into mils for you and then you can use the information in the firing table accordingly; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question to me? I have no argument with the table. I'm just saying, it doesn't matter because it affects only distance, not divergence from the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's continue down. Let's go to the M52 firing table, which is 65 ter 33685 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you think that going through the tables could be finished in the next two minutes? If not, then I suggest we take a break first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, Witness, we'll continue after the break with the mils and the degrees, but for the time being, take a break, and the usher will escort you out, and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I'll briefly deal with a procedural matter, which is about remaining MFIs from Jasmin Odobasic. On 7 September 2015, the Defence tendered a statement of Jasmin Odobasic and 12 associated exhibits into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis. The Prosecution responded on 21 September, not opposing the motion and tendering three additional documents. On 15 December, the Chamber conditionally admitted the statement and 14 documents pending the filing of an attestation and declaration in compliance with Rule 92 bis. Subsequently, the Defence decided to present the evidence of Odobasic in court. On 26 April, the Chamber ordered that the remaining Defence witnesses, including Odobasic, commence their testimony during the week of the 30th of May at the latest. This can be found at transcript pages 43702 and -703. As the week of the 30th of May has passed and the Defence has not brought Odobasic to testify, the Chamber hereby understands that the Defence is not proceeding with the presentation of the witness's evidence. And the Chamber would like to know whether it understands this situation well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It does not understand the situation well. We are exploring methods of obtaining that evidence as was communicated to Chamber's staff. In a meeting with the Office of the Prosecutor wherein both the Prosecutor and I were on the phone with Chamber's staff and advised of that. I apologise that we did not do a formal filing after that. We've been trying to explore many options with the various departments of this Tribunal and the capabilities of the witness, given the multiple medical documents that have been sent by this witness. Since we're in open session, I won't go into the details of the same, but the Defence talked to the Prosecution again yesterday after court about the various possibilities of proceeding with that evidence, and we anticipate having a filing seeking to have that evidence introduced without the necessity of hearing the witness. So the evidence will still be sought to be introduced into -- into the trial record without the attendance of the witness. So I can clarify with respect to that, that the attendance of the witness will likely not be -- will likely not be necessary and that we will seek to have the written evidence of the witness introduced by one of the rules available for the same, and we -- based upon out discussions with the Prosecution, we hope to have a filing which will have a portion that will be a stipulation by the parties as to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then, we'll wait and see that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This history now, as I started saying, goes back to the 7th of September of last year, when the Defence tendered the statement of Mr. Odobasic.
